newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh jurors confront death penalty issue.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh jurors confront death penalty issue.

text.p: Prospective jurors in the Oklahoma City bombing trial publicly wrestled with their conscience on Wednesday over the most private of issues -- whether they could sentence another human being to death.

They are being closely quizzed on whether they could order the execution of Timothy McVeigh if the Gulf War veteran is convicted of the April 19, 1995, attack on the Alfred P. Murrah federal building. The blast killed 168 people.

For some potential jurors, the question has produced intense soul searching while others have said it would not bother them at all, even if they had to look McVeigh in the eye after pronouncing sentence.

Meanwhile, lawyers for news organisations covering the trial filed legal papers to stop Federal Judge Richard Matsch from holding daily closed door conferences with lawyers to decide which jurors to dismiss.

A court hearing has been set for Thursday before Matsch, who has gone out of his way to keep the jury selection as private as possible, including referring to jurors by numbers rather than by name and constructing a partition in his court so the public can only hear them speak and not see them.
In most trials, jurors are chosen or rejected in open court.

During questioning by defence and prosecution lawyers, most jurors have admitted that being called for the Oklahoma City bombing case marked the first time in their lives that they have had to think deeply about the death penalty.
One woman called it a troubling experience. "I've been thinking about this probably through the night last night," the IBM computer expert with strong religious views said.

The woman, finishing up testimony she had begun on Tuesday, said her Christian beliefs would prohibit her from giving McVeigh the death penalty if he was convicted. "I don't feel capable of throwing that first stone ... human justice is imperfect, God's justice is perfect," she said.
A woman who worked on a farm had equally strong views in favour of the death penalty, saying she "would be for the death penalty for anybody that kills other people."
Most jurors said they would be prepared to vote for execution if McVeigh were convicted and the evidence justified it.
Anyone sitting in a death penalty case must be willing to consider voting for it. People opposed to capital punishment will be disqualified.

Tom Kight, whose 23-year-old stepdaughter died in the bombing, was sympathetic to the jurors' dilemma. "The fact that you as an individual could be put on a team that would decide a man's fate that could be death I think is a very tough decision," he told reporters.

The pace of jury selection was slightly swifter than the snail's pace of the first two days. Matsch nudged lawyers along and admonished them for repetitious questioning. So far, 19 potential jurors have been questioned from a jury panel of 352.
McVeigh followed the proceedings closely. Occasionally, he whispered to his attorneys and passed notes to them.
